source.title: CRaFT: Circuit-Guided Refusal Feature Selection via Cross-Layer Transcoders
source.authors: Su-Hyeon Kim; Hyundong Jin; Ye-Jin Lee; Youran Han

record.tranche_reason: The study implements a Refusal-Direction baseline based on the original harmful-versus-harmless direction method, applies the removal intervention to a new model, and measures jailbreak and capability outcomes. The implementation is adapted and does not test the original all-layer, all-position intervention.
record.gate_note: The Refusal-Direction baseline’s intervention results are recorded. CRaFT’s own circuit-feature steering and its cross-model results are included as findings about a different refusal intervention, not as tests of the difference-in-means direction. Feature values used only for selection, cited findings, and results for unrelated prompt-based or SAE baselines are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study runs the official Arditi et al. Refusal-Direction code (harmful minus harmless difference-in-means, direction removed at inference) on gemma-3-1b-it. It reports both refusal-bypass rates (LlamaGuard-4 ASR, StrongREJECT judge) and general capability (MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval) against no-intervention baselines. These results bear directly on V1's ablation and capability-preservation claims. The method is adapted: the KL threshold is relaxed and the induce-refusal filter is disabled. The rest of the paper is CRaFT, a different, CLT-feature intervention.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that circuit-guided (influence-based, boundary-critical) CLT feature selection beats activation-based and dense-direction steering for jailbreaking, giving more specific harmful completions while preserving capability. They state that the dense refusal direction is entangled with general computation and collapses gemma-3-1b-it's capability. Cross-model gains require model-specific features and multipliers.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts the official Refusal-Direction implementation to Gemma-3-1b-it and retains its harmful/harmless-pair training procedure, but changes filtering thresholds, disables the induce-refusal threshold, and uses a selected intervention layer rather than testing projection at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: For CRaFT, attack outcomes vary with steering strength and the number of jointly steered features; transfer models require model-specific features and multiplier selection. The Llama transfer setting also uses an extended boundary-token set.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling down a single circuit-selected CLT feature (L3_F289) on gemma-3-1b-it raises LG4 ASR to 47–65% and Judge scores to about 3/5. Capability stays within ±0.5 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single sparse CLT feature, selected by logit influence near the refusal boundary, can bypass refusal with little capability loss.

fits_no_version.finding: CRaFT with features reselected per model raises ASR on gemma-3-270m-it and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Multipliers are tuned per model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The CRaFT feature-selection pipeline generalizes across CLT-backed small instruct models.

record.problems: The Refusal-Direction behavioral evaluation includes an unsafe-response classifier that the authors say can misclassify degenerate or non-actionable outputs; its rubric scores are mixed. The method is adapted, and only a selected intervention layer is reported. Capability comparisons use same-backend baselines, and the MMLU direction-removal score is affected by parseability failure. Several behavioral results have no reported error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Refusal-Direction results beyond the four benchmark ASR/Judge pairs and four capability measures were reported. CRaFT feature-selection diagnostics, hyperparameter sweeps, and runtime results were left out because they do not test the difference-in-means direction; the principal CRaFT benchmark and cross-model outcome rows are retained.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. The refusal-substring score that the original pipeline uses is not reported.
Entire version: no test of whether prompt jailbreaks act by suppressing the direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation.
Cross-model runs reselect CRaFT features per model; there is no transfer of the refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is 'tests' only through the Refusal-Direction baseline, which is a T4-style comparison inside a method paper. The direction was obtained with relaxed filters: KL threshold raised to 10 and the induce-refusal check disabled. The capability collapse may reflect that adaptation rather than the method as specified. Appendix C lists 'selected intervention layer: 14'. It is unclear whether ablation was applied only there or, as in the official code, at all layers and positions, so the record's claim of single-layer ablation is not confirmed. No error bars for the baseline. LG4 ASR is known by the authors to count degenerate text as unsafe.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, or projecting it out at every layer and position. Capability preservation is tested for the adapted removal baseline.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested; the baseline removes a direction during inference.

Tests a direction-removal intervention as a jailbreak baseline, not whether other attacks work by suppressing that direction. Does not train against its ablation or test robustness from such training.
Does not directly compare whether refusal is encoded by one direction versus an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus others.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Cross-model results reselect model-specific circuit features; they do not test transfer of the difference-in-means direction, language transfer, or base-to-instruct transfer.
Does not vary refusal-training data, method, or timing to test whether training determines whether a single removable direction exists.

relation.reason: Its own Refusal-Direction runs on gemma-3-1b-it report refusal-bypass rates and capability against a no-intervention baseline, which bears directly on V1.

tranche.reason: Runs the official Arditi et al. code: harmful-minus-harmless direction, removed from the residual stream at inference (layer 14). Measures a LlamaGuard-family unsafe rate plus capability benchmarks, as the original did. The loosened filters are a protocol change but leave the method the same.

source_check.notes: Refusal-Direction is only a baseline in this CRaFT paper. It was run with the KL threshold relaxed to 10 and the induce-refusal filter disabled; the authors call the original thresholds overly restrictive for gemma-3-1b-it. No refusal rate is reported for its outputs, and on SorryBench its judge score falls 1.17→0.44, below no-attack. Capability numbers use the HF backend, and the MMLU 0.00 is a parse collapse under an 8-token budget.

statements.correction: gemma-3-1b-it, Refusal-Direction, layer 14, KL threshold relaxed to 10, induce-refusal filter off. LG4 ASR: JailBreak 5.0→35.0, HarmBench 9.5→35.0, AdvBench 0.4→43.6, SorryBench 12.0→22.0, average 6.7→33.9. Authors: the original thresholds were 'overly restrictive for this smaller model'.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right. The statement leaves out HarmBench (9.5%→35.0%). LG4 ASR is an unsafe-label rate, and the paper gives no refusal rate for Refusal-Direction outputs, so 'leaves substantial refusal' is inferred from that unsafe-label rate.
